Terror
TER-er
n.
Latin terror, “great fear, dread,” from terrere (to frighten). Renders the Hebrew émāh, “dread, terror,” and the Greek phobos, “fear, terror,” especially in its objective sense of that-which-is-to-be-feared.

Biblical Definition

Terror in Scripture has two distinct biblical registers, and the contemporary believer often hears only one. The terror of the LORD is the apostolic name for the awe-evoking, judgment-shaped reality of the holy God Himself, set forth as the proper motive of evangelistic urgency: knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men. Paul does not name this terror to embarrass the gospel but to anchor its urgency: the holy God who will judge the world in righteousness through Christ is no less holy and no less judging because His mercy is wide; the terror of being on the wrong side of His day is real, and the apostle’s persuasion of men is grounded partly in that terror as well as in the love of Christ that compels him. The Old Testament prophets uniformly speak of the LORD’s terror as His characteristic effect upon the unrepentant: the day of the LORD cometh, cruel both with wrath and fierce anger... and they shall be afraid: pangs and sorrows shall take hold of them. The second register is the fear of terror the saint is to refuse: be not afraid of their terror, neither be troubled; fear not their fear, neither be afraid; the threats of the world’s power, the intimidations of the persecutor, the dread-inducing pressures of the spirit of the age are not to terrify the saint who has set apart the Lord God in his heart. Peter explicitly weaves the two: Sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear: Having a good conscience. The biblical doctrine therefore holds two terrors in their proper places: the terror of the LORD, which is the gospel-grounded urgency motive of evangelism and the personal awe that becomes the regenerate soul before its holy Maker; and the terror-of-men, which is the world’s attempt to intimidate the saint into silence and unfaithfulness, and which the saint refuses precisely because his heart has been sanctified by the greater terror of God. Where the contemporary church has lost the doctrine of God’s holiness and judgment, the first terror has shrunk to nothing; where the contemporary church has compromised before cultural pressure, the second terror has grown to occupy the space the first ought to fill. The recovery is to restore the proper proportions: terror of God, and the freedom from terror of man that the first terror produces.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines TERROR as extreme fear; violent dread; fright; fear that agitates the body and mind; that which excites dread; in scripture, both the awe-evoking reality of the holy God Himself and the world’s threats which the saint is commanded not to fear.

expand to see more

TERROR, n. — 1. Extreme fear; violent dread; fright; fear that agitates the body and mind. 2. That which excites dread; the cause of extreme fear. Rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil (Rom 13:3). 3. In scripture, the awe-evoking reality of the holy God Himself, as in the terror of the Lord (2 Cor 5:11).

Key Scripture

2 Corinthians 5:11 — "Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men; but we are made manifest unto God; and I trust also are made manifest in your consciences."

Isaiah 8:12-13 — "Neither fear ye their fear, nor be afraid. Sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread."

1 Peter 3:14-15 — "But and if ye suffer for righteousness’ sake, happy are ye: and be not afraid of their terror, neither be troubled; But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts..."

Hebrews 10:31 — "It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God."

Modern Corruption

Terror is corrupted, in the contemporary church, by the loss of the doctrine of God’s holiness and judgment that has shrunk the first terror (the terror of the Lord) to nothing—and by the cultural pressure that has grown the second terror (the fear of man) to occupy the space the first ought to fill, producing a Christianity that fears the world’s disapproval and does not fear the LORD.

expand to see more

The first terror—the terror of the Lord that Paul names as part of the motive of his evangelism—has shrunk to nearly nothing in much of the contemporary church. The doctrine of God’s holiness has been muted; the doctrine of God’s judgment has been quietly retired or eschatologically postponed beyond practical reach; the diagnostic seriousness of it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God has been domesticated into something gentler. The result is a Christianity in which no one is persuaded, in part, by the terror of the Lord—because the terror has been theologically defanged. Recover the doctrine of God’s holiness and judgment, recover the apostolic candor about the terror that motivates persuasion, and the gospel recovers its urgency and the saint his proper awe before the holy God whose mercy he has tasted.

The second terror has grown to fill the space the first ought to occupy. The contemporary believer often fears the world’s disapproval intensely (the social-media pile-on, the cancellation, the cultural marginalization, the loss of employment or platform for confessing biblical truth) and fears the LORD’s displeasure mildly or not at all. The apostles and prophets reverse the proportions. Sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread. Be not afraid of their terror, neither be troubled. The greater terror frees the soul from the lesser: the saint who is rightly awed by the holy God can stand calmly before the world’s threats; the saint who fears the world and does not fear the LORD has reversed the proportions and will compromise wherever the world’s pressure exceeds the LORD’s felt weight. Recover the proper proportions, and the courage of confession returns, the freedom of speech returns, the steadiness of the faithful witness returns—all of it the proper fruit of the first terror sanctifying the heart and crowding the second terror out.

Hebrew Roots

Hebrew émāh (dread, terror) and pachad (dread); Greek phobos (fear, terror, both subjective fear and the objective thing-feared)—the two biblical terrors held in proper proportion: terror of God, and the freedom from terror of man that the first terror produces.

expand to see more

Hebrew émāh (H367) — dread, terror (Gen 15:12; Ex 15:16; 23:27).

Hebrew pachad (H6343) — dread, terror (the “dread of the LORD” word).

Greek phobos (G5401) — fear, terror; both subjective fear and the objective thing-feared (2 Cor 5:11; 1 Pet 3:14).

Greek ekphobos (G1630) — very afraid, terrified (Heb 12:21, Moses at Sinai).

Usage

"Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men—Paul anchors evangelistic urgency in the apostolic candor about God’s holiness and judgment."

"Be not afraid of their terror, neither be troubled; But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts—the greater terror frees the saint from the lesser."

"Contemporary church has shrunk the first terror and grown the second; recovery is to restore the proper proportions—terror of God, freedom from terror of man."
